title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: ChatGPT Assessment for Anatomy Course
venue: International Journal of Management Information Systems and Computer Science
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can perform as well as or better than university students on an anatomy examination. The motivating question is not about writing feedback or secondary education, but about the comparative performance of a newly released AI system in a higher-education assessment context. The authors position the study as an early exploration of ChatGPT’s educational potential and risks, including concerns about cheating and the future role of AI in learning.

The approach was a descriptive comparison between ChatGPT and students on the same 40-item multiple-choice anatomy test. Thirty-seven students from the Faculty of Health Sciences at a state university in Turkey, who had previously taken an anatomy course, received four weeks of instruction on a specific anatomy topic and then completed the exam. The researchers also entered the same test questions into ChatGPT and compared the number of correct and incorrect responses using descriptive statistics.

The study population was undergraduate health sciences students in a single Turkish public university. The context appears to be a course-based instructional setting focused on anatomy, but the paper does not study classroom integration of ChatGPT as a feedback tool for student writing. It also does not address grades 9-12 students, student-authored drafts, or ChatGPT-generated feedback on writing.

The main finding was that ChatGPT answered 27 of 40 questions correctly (67.5%), whereas students averaged 21.1 correct answers (52.8%). The authors conclude that ChatGPT outperformed the average student on this anatomy test and may have promise as an educational tool. However, they also note risks such as academic integrity concerns and limitations in interpreting visual materials. For the retrieval topic of secondary students receiving ChatGPT feedback on writing drafts, no relevant subgroup, moderator, transfer, self-efficacy, adverse-effect, follow-up, unaided writing, revision skill, metacognition, voice, plagiarism, or overreliance evidence is reported.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small descriptive comparison study with a stated method and numerical results, but no randomization, no control for confounding, no inferential statistics, and limited relevance to the requested K-12 draft-feedback use case. It meets only minimal credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a performance difference favoring ChatGPT on one anatomy multiple-choice test, but impact is unclear because no effect size, variance, or causal design is provided, and the outcome is not a direct educational intervention effect on learners.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as a conversational AI respondent to answer 40 multiple-choice anatomy exam questions, and its score was compared with undergraduate health sciences students' scores.

finding.finding_summary: In a descriptive comparison in a Turkish undergraduate anatomy course, ChatGPT answered 27 of 40 multiple-choice questions correctly (67.5%), while 37 students averaged 21.1 correct answers (52.8%). This suggests ChatGPT outperformed the average student on anatomy knowledge assessment, but no inferential statistics, effect sizes, subgroup analyses, or delayed outcomes were reported.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice anatomy test score (40 items), correct and incorrect responses, percent score
finding.study_size: n=37 students; ChatGPT single system comparison

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may create opportunities for higher education while also posing risks to exam integrity because it can generate realistic answers quickly. However, these institutional implications were discussed conceptually rather than directly measured, with no empirical data on cheating, plagiarism, governance, or policy outcomes.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; discussion of academic integrity and exam validity risks
finding.study_size: n=37 students; no institutional outcome sample
